frase_gancho.texto: A skull with red rays that represents the Sun as it dies.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the Sun that goes out, we move on to the fire that must never go out. Step up to the stone old man who carries a brazier on his head: the Old God, whom you already met in clay.

guion_corto.texto: In front of you is an andesite disk, more than a meter tall, with traces of red paint. At the center, a human skull with its mouth open and its tongue sticking out. Around it, a halo folded like paper or like rays of sunlight. It was found in 1964 in front of the Pyramid of the Sun. It is interpreted as the Sun as it sets in the west: the Earth swallows it to light the world of the dead, and then lets it be reborn in the east. For the people of Teotihuacán, death was not the end, but part of a cycle. An image that is cold and luminous at the same time.

guion_largo.texto:
Archaeologists found it in 1964, the same year this museum was inaugurated, in front of the Pyramid of the Sun. It is made of andesite, a volcanic stone, and it still preserves traces of red paint, the color of Teotihuacán: walls and floors were painted red, and the entire city shone. That red, almost erased today, was part of the message.

Notice that this is not a “sad” skull. Its mouth is open, its teeth are showing, and its tongue sticks out, as if it were speaking, or singing, or devouring. The halo that surrounds it is made of slanted grooves, and it has been compared to folded paper, to a fan of feathers, and to rays of sunlight. That is why it is linked to the death of the Sun: a skull that frightens and lights up at the same time.

For the peoples of Mesoamerica, the Sun died every day. At nightfall it descended to the world of the dead, and the next morning it had to be born again. We know a great deal about this idea from the Mexica, who told that the Sun rose accompanied by warriors who had died in combat and bid farewell accompanied by women who had died in childbirth. It is likely that its roots are much older, like those of Teotihuacán.

There is a detail that repeats: the tongue. In the Mexica Hall, the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol) has at its center a face whose tongue is a flint knife, a symbol of sacrifice. We do not know whether there is a direct connection, but we do know that the Mexica admired Teotihuacán, took ideas from it, and even gave it the name by which we know it. When you see that face, remember this one.

Teotihuacán did not hide death. There were burials in homes, tombs beneath floors, offerings in temples: the city sustained itself by giving life in order to receive life. But there was also an idea of renewal. Important dead people became ancestors who protected the family, something you will see in the masks and the braziers that follow.

It is not known for certain what this disk was used for. It may have been part of an altar or of a building in front of the pyramid. The fact that it was found there suggests a solar ritual, but that is a hypothesis. Its size, more than a meter, indicates that it could be seen well from some distance, and the red paint made it even more striking in the light of the valley.

The Pyramid of the Sun is one of the largest in the Americas, and beneath it there is a tunnel that ends in a cave-shaped chamber which, according to several archaeologists, may have been what made the place sacred. Many Mesoamerican cultures saw in caves the entrance to the underworld and the origin of peoples. A sun that dies before a pyramid built over a cave: the image is round.

That is why it is best to look at this disk as a clock: a sun that hides and returns, again and again, while the city rises, transforms, and, in its own time, also goes out.

texto: Look at the skull and the tongue sticking out of its mouth
Find the traces of red paint on the stone
Notice the rays of the halo: do they look like folded paper or sunlight?

texto.Origin: Teotihuacán, State of Mexico (plaza in front of the Pyramid of the Sun)
texto.Dimensions: 1.26 m high x 1.02 m wide x 0.25 m thick
texto.Discovery: Found in 1964 during excavations in front of the Pyramid of the Sun

texto.pregunta: Myth: Ancient peoples saw death only with terror.
texto.respuesta: Reality: For many peoples of Mesoamerica, death was part of a cycle, like the Sun that sets and rises again; this skull can be read as a symbol of that return.
